list.listitem: Chest pain may represent serious cardiovascular disease or other less serious conditions. C

Initial evaluation of patients with chest pain should focus on the nature of chest pain (typical, atypical, or non-cardiac, see ), anginal symptoms, physical findings, 12-lead ECG, and serum cardiac markers unless another cause is readily apparent from the history and examination. C
An algorithm for the evaluation of patients with chest pain is shown in and .

Exercise treadmill stress testing can help exclude coronary artery disease (CAD) in low-risk patients with chest pain, while exercise or chemical stress tests with cardiac imaging is more sensitive and specific for CAD in higher risk patients. B

Common noncardiac causes for chest pain include musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, psychiatric, and pulmonary disorders. Rare but life-threatening causes that should always be considered include pulmonary embolismand aortic aneurysm.C

background.definition: Chest pain from angina or CAD often is deep chest discomfort associated with exertion or emotional stress and relieved with rest or nitroglycerin, but angina may present with jaw or arm pain, dyspnea, or sweating. Pain that is sharp and stabbing, well localized, and either very brief or long-lasting is less likely to be cardiac.

list.listitem: 1% to 2% of outpatient visits are for chest pain.

The prevalence of myocardial infarction (MI) varies with the setting: 1% to 2% among primary care outpatients, compared with 13% unstable CAD or MI among patients seen in the emergency room for chest pain.
CAD leads to $150 billion annually in direct and indirect costs.
Chest pain is a common cause of Emergency Department visits in the United States.
CAD is the leading cause of death in the United States.

A prospective study of 399 patients presenting to family physicians found that musculoskeletal (20%), reflux (14%), costochondritis (13%), and stable angina (10%) were the most common causes; only 1.5% had unstable angina or acute MI.
Panic attacks are a common but infrequently recognized cause in primary care practice.
Common causes for chest pain in emergency care are: cardiovascular (50%) and muscular (10%), as well as pulmonary, psychiatric, and gastrointestinal.

The pathophysiology varies with the cause; cardiovascular causes are discussed below.
Reduced cardiac perfusion due to partially occluding coronary artery thrombus that developed on a disrupted atherosclerotic plaque. The most common cause of a disrupted atherosclerotic plaque is arterial inflammation leading to plaque expansion and destabilization. Focal coronary artery spasm. Severe coronary artery narrowing without spasm or thrombus. Coronary artery dissection. Secondary angina due to increased myocardial oxygen requirements, reduced coronary blood flow (eg, hypotension), or reduced oxygen delivery (eg, anemia).

The USPSTF recommends against screening with resting or exercise electrocardiography (ECG) for the prediction of coronary heart disease (CHD) events in asymptomatic adults at low risk for CHD events. B

The USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening with resting or exercise ECG for the prediction of CHD events in asymptomatic adults at intermediate or high risk for CHD events. B
Most asymptomatic low-risk individuals with a positive exercise stress test will not have clinically significant CAD when subjected to angiography (positive predictive value 20%). C

For patients with chest pain, determine whether the pain is substernal, radiating, exertional, and/or relieved with rest or nitroglycerin. Ask about associated symptoms such as dyspnea and diaphoresis. C
Obtain a 12-lead ECG to evaluate for acute or chronic ischemia. For patients at risk for coronary disease obtain biomarkers and/or refer for coronary CT angiography or stress test. C
Serum cardiac markers can detect MI and predict death or MI over the next 30 days in patients with chest pain suspicious for cardiac ischemia. A
Plain exercise stress testing can help exclude CAD in low-risk patients; exercise or chemical stress testing is more sensitive and specific for CAD in higher risk patients. B
Important noncardiac causes of chest pain to consider include PE, GERD, pneumothorax, aortic dissection, pericarditis, pleuritis, costochondritis, pneumothorax, zoster, and depression. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Anginal (ischemic) chest pain or acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
Differential.Differential_Features: Substernal, exertional, relieved with rest or nitroglycerin
Heartburn, no ECG changes, worse when recumbent
Tachypnea, hypocarbia and hypoxemia, clear CXR
Severe pain, wide mediastinum on CXR
Pain changes with posture and respiration, widespread ST changes
Continual heaviness, no ECG changes, not affected by exertion

list.listitem: See section on Clinical Decision Rules for validated strategies to assess pretest probability, the risk of coronary disease, the risk of MI or unstable angina, and prognosis. See chapters on pulmonary embolismand thoracic aneurysmfor a more detailed discussion of those conditions. A 4-point clinical decision rule for ACS performs similarly to the judgement of a general practitioner.
Prediction rules are only moderately accurate in predicting CAD in primary care settings—performing better in "ruling out" the diagnosis than "ruling in."

Chest pain that is stabbing, pleuritic, positional, or reproducible with palpation is low risk for acute coronary syndrome (ACS), chest pain that is not related to exertion, or is in a small infra-mammary are of the chest is probably also low risk for ACS, while chest pain that is exertional, radiating to one or both arms, similar to or worse than prior cardiac chest pain, or associated with nausea, vomiting or diaphoresis is high risk for ACS.

American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association criteria for risk of unstable angina are shown in . CAD: A study of more than 1000 consecutive primary care patients with nontraumatic chest pain found that the following 5 items were the best predictors of heart disease as the cause: age over 55 in men or 65 in women; a history of known CAD, occlusive vascular disease, or cerebrovascular disease; pain worse during exercise; pain not reproducible by palpation; and the patient assumes pain is of cardiac origin. These predictors have been incorporated into the Marburg Heart Score, which can be used to estimate the likelihood of CAD when a patient presents with chest pain. PE: global clinical assessment by an experienced attending physician (using the history and physical examination) is the best single predictor of PE. Individual signs and symptoms are of relatively little value; use validated clinical decision rules in the evaluation, like the Wells, Pisa, or Geneva scores. Thoracic artery aneurysm: a pulse deficit is the single best predictor of the presence of thoracic artery aneurysm, while absence of chest pain is the best item to rule it out. Chest wall pain: This includes costochondritis, costosternal syndrome, and Tietze's syndrome. A German study of 1212 adults older than 35 years with nontraumatic chest pain presenting to a primary care doctor found that the following were independent predictors of a final diagnosis of chest wall pain: localized muscle tension, stinging pain, pain reproducible by palpation, and absence of cough. However, even the presence of 3 or 4 factors only had a 77% positive predictive value for chest wall pain, so it is important to consider other causes even when chest wall pain is most likely.

In the outpatient primary care setting, noncardiac causes are most common (eg, musculoskeletal chest pain, reflux disease, panic disorder, costochondritis). Once cardiac causes, PE, and aneurysm have been ruled out, evaluate the patient for those conditions.

In children with chest pain, exertional chest pain was the most important predictor of a serious underlying cause. Most patients with a serious cause could be identified by a detailed history and physical, an ECG, and then additional testing for those with abnormalities.

Initial evaluation should include ECG in all patients with chest pain. The sum of the ST segment deviation of all 12 leads is a novel test for acute MI (LR = 20 for ≥14.1 mm, and LR = 10 for ≥12.4 mm).

Stress testing with myocardial perfusion imaging is approximately 88% accurate for diagnosis of CAD in patients with chest pain. Only a small fraction of patients referred for stress testing from the emergency department to evaluate chest pain will have obstructive coronary disease on cardiac catheterization.

Acute MI can be diagnosed by elevated levels oftroponin T, troponin I, or serial ECGs. The sensitivity of troponin increases during the first 6 to 8 hours following the onset of chest pain. New highly sensitive troponin I and T assays are more useful within 3 hours of onset of pain, in particular they are more sensitive and have better negative predictive value (97%-99%) than older assays.

In patients with chest pain lasting less than 12 hours, no recent MI, normal or near-normal ECG, and normal troponin I or T at the time of admission and 4 and 6 hours later, only 0.3% had death or MI within 30 days.

High risk clinical features for ACS include hemodynamic instability, typical crescendo angina, >20 minutes of prior angina at rest, ongoing pain, an abnormal electrocardiogram, or abnormal troponin T level. Absence of these findings is associated with a good clinical outcome.

In patients with acute chest discomfort, use of sensitive troponin I and highly senstitive troponin T methods lead to significant improvement in the early diagnostic accuracy of acute coronary syndrome. High-sensitivity troponin has significantly higher early sensitivity and negative predictive value for the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction, but is associated with lower specificity and lower positive predictive value.

An algorithm incorporating high-sensitivity cardiac troponin baseline values and absolute changes over 2 hours allows triage towards safe "rule out" or accurate "rule in" of acute myocardial infarction in most patients, with only 20% requiring prolonged monitoring.

A 2-hour protocol of initial electrocardiography (ECG), troponin testing, and Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) scoring, followed by repeat testing in 2 hours, can allow almost twice as many patients with chest pain and symptoms consistent with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) being discharged within 6 hours of presentation to an emergency department.

A protocol developed in 9604 patients and validated in 13,047 patients uses a disk-shaped display to identify patients at low and high risk of acute MI. For example, a patient with an initial troponin I level of less than 4 ng/L at ED presentation and a second value (1 hour later) that has risen by less than 3 ng/L has a negative predictive value of 99.7% (95% CI 99.4 - 99.8) for MI and a 0.2% 30-day risk of MI or death. The calculator is also available at www.compass-mi.com. The long-term risks for patients who have MI ruled out are also presented. For example, a patient with an initial troponin I level of 2.5 ng/L has a 2% 1-year risk and 3.5% 2-year risk of MI or death, compared to 0.9% and 2.3%, respectively, in a general population sample of patients.
Negative testing with coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) allows for a safe discharge in patients with low to intermediate risk for acute coronary syndromes.

In patients with chest pain and suspected CAD, a strategy of initial CT angiogram does not improve clinical outcomes over 2 years of followup, when compared with initial functional testing. In intermediate-risk patients, coronary CT angiography is similar to myocardial perfusion imaging for identifying patients suitable for invasive testing. One study of CT angiography found that this test reduced the likelihood of non-fatal MI in the follow up period.

An individual patient data meta-analysis found that CT angiography was accurate for diagnosis of obstructive CAD in patients with chest pain, with an AUROCC of 0.90. Sensitivity was 95% and specificity 79%. It was most useful when the pretest probability of CAD was between 7% and 67%.

Patients with chest pain who are appropriately evaluated in an emergency room and do not have an acute myocardial infarction, are at very low risk of experiening myocardial infarction in short and long term followup, and deferral of early non-invasive testing appears to be reasonable.

Aortic dissection: while transthoracic echocardiography is convenient, it is much less sensitive than CT or MRI. Transesophageal echocardiography is an alternative mode of imaging if qualified operators are immediately available and the patient has significant contraindications to CT scanning (nephropathy or hemodynamic instability).
Copeptin is the plasma stable c-terminal part of AVP and is released with cardiac stress earlier than troponin.

A negative copeptin associated with a negative HS-TnT in a patient presenting with a low GRACE score may expedite the diagnostic exclusion of non-ST+ ACS; this is not used commonly in clinical practice.

The AROMI trial randomized 4351 patients being transported by EMS with suspected AMI to prehospital measurement of copeptin with a standard 3 hours hsTnT protocol. All patients were managed in the ED. Those in the copeptin arm went home about an hour early and at one month there was no difference in major adverse cardiac events (risk difference 0.45, 95% CI -2.5 to 1.7 favoring copeptin).

The Framingham cardiac risk profile and the Pryor prediction rule predict the risk of significant CAD in outpatients based on age and gender, risk factors, and basic diagnostic testing. They estimate risk for outpatients in general, not those with chest pain, and are not useful in assessment of a particular episode of chest pain.
The pretest probability that chest pain represents CAD can be predicted based on age, gender, and chest pain characteristics.
In patients with a normal or near-normal ECG, age, gender, and type of pain predict the likelihood of MI.
The Marburg Heart Score can predict the risk of CAD for primary care patients presenting with non-traumatic chest pain.
The Goldman algorithm has been well validated and can help predict which patients are at higher risk of MI; it can be used to guide decision regarding admission to the hospital and CCU.

The Duke Treadmill Score can predict the 7-year risk of cardiac mortality in patients with chest pain and nonspecific ST abnormalities who are evaluated with stress ECG testing. A similar rule that incorporates the results of single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging can predict the annual cardiac death rate for patients undergoing adenosine stress testing.

The Vancouver Chest Pain Rule can be used for the identification of low risk patients presenting to emergency departments with symptoms of possible acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and will reduce the proportion of patients requiring lengthy assessment.
A chest pain evaluation algorithm that incorportates high-sensitivity troponin (hsTnT) can help to rapidly triage patients in one hour into high, medium, and low risk groups.

Among patients with chest pain presenting to the ED, the HEART score can predict their likelihood of ACS as the cause with high sensitivity and high negative predictive value according to a meta-analysis of 25 studies.
The HEAR score is a version of the score that does not require troponin. It incorporates history, ECG, age and risk factors only.
Instruct patients with symptoms representing a high likelihood of unstable angina and patients with known CAD experiencing worsening chest pain to call 911.
See and summarize an approach to the initial management of patients with chest pain and possible coronary artery disease recommended by the European Society of Cardiology.

In the ED, rapidly assess patients presenting with acute chest discomfort for the risk of ACS (MI or unstable angina) based on history, physical examination, 12-lead ECG, and cardiac biomarkers. Provide O2 per nasal cannula, aspirin, and IV access. If the initial ECG is nondiagnostic and the patient remains symptomatic, order serial ECG recordings at 15- to 30-minute intervals to evaluate for development of ischemic changes. Remeasure biomarkers between 8 and 12 hours after symptom onset in patients with negative cardiac biomarkers within 6 hours of the onset of symptoms consistent with ACS. Also consider important noncardiac causes (eg, PE, aneurysm, pneumothorax) in patients with chest pain. See for a guide to admission decisions based on the validated Goldman algorithm.

In the primary care setting, refer patients at risk for a cardiac cause to the appropriate setting where it can be appropriately evaluated. The pretest probability in patients with stable chest pain symptoms is shown in . European Society of Cardiology guidelines recommend the following based on the pretest probability of obstructive coronary disease in Table 3: < 15%: no further testing; 15 to 65%: exercise or non-invasive imaging test to evaluate for coronary artery disease; 66% to 85%: non-invasive imaging functional test; 85% or more: assume coronary artery disease is present. The likelihood of a cardiac cause in primary care patients presenting with chest pain can also be evaluated using the Marburg Heart Score.

ACC/AHA guidelines for evaluation of chest pain (2021) emphasize that pain in extremeties or jaw and shortness of breath should be considered chest pain equivalents. Hith sensitivity troponins are preferred over other ests. Patients who are low risk with acute or stable chest pain do not necessarily need urgent diagnostic testing; shared decision making is encouraged. The use of "atypical chest pain" is discouraged; if heart disease is not suspected, it should e called "noncardiac". Use of chest pain pathways is mandatory. After exam and ECG, patients should be classified as STEMI, pericarditis, NSTEMI, new arrthymia, or nondiagnostic/normal. The latter require further evaluation and monitoring.

caption.strong: Recommended Strategies for Determining Where to Admit Patients With Acute Chest Pain for Treatment of Ongoing Life-Threatening Conditions.

feature.feature_body:
Location Indication
Intensive care unit One of the following:
Substantial ischemic ECG changes in 2 or more leads that are not known to be old
ST-segment elevation ≥1 mm or Q-waves of 0.04 seconds or more
ST-segment depression ≥1 mm or T-wave inversion consistent with the presence of ischemia
Any 2 of the following conditions, with or without substantial ECG changes:
Coronary artery disease known to be unstable (in terms of frequency, duration, intensity, or failure to respond to usual measures)
Systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg
Serious new arrhythmias (new-onset atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, sustained supraventricular tachycardia, second-degree or complete heart block, or sustained or recurrent ventricular arrhythmias)
Rales above the bases
Intermediate care unit Any of the following conditions but not meeting criteria for intensive care:
Coronary artery disease known to be unstable
Systolic blood pressure <110 mm Hg
Rales above the bases
Major arrhythmias (new-onset atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, sustained supraventricular tachycardia, second-degree or complete heart block, or sustained or recurrent ventricular arrhythmias)
New-onset typical ischemic heart disease that meets the clinical criteria for unstable angina and that occurs at rest or with minimal exertion
Evaluation or observation unit New-onset symptoms that may be consistent with ischemic heart disease but are not associated with ECG changes or a convincing diagnosis of unstable ischemic heart disease at rest or with minimal exertion
Known coronary artery disease whose presentation does not suggest a true worsening but with further observation is thought to be beneficial, commonly because a benign diagnosis cannot be established
Home with office follow-up in 7 to 10 days to determine whether further testing is needed Other conditions
From Lee TH, Goldman L. Evaluation of the patient with acute chest pain. Radiol Clin North Am 2010 Jul;48(4):745–755.

caption.strong: ACC/AHA Criteria for Risk in Patients with Unstable Angina.

feature.feature_body: High likelihood of unstable angina (any of the following): Chest or left arm pain or discomfort reproducing prior angina Known history of coronary artery disease Hypotension, diaphoresis, pulmonary edema, or rales Intermediate likelihood of unstable angina (absence of high-likelihood criteria and presence of any of the following): Chest or left arm pain or discomfort as primary symptom Age >70 years Male, history of diabetes or extracardiac vascular disease Male, history of diabetes or extracardiac vascular disease Low likelihood of unstable angina: Probable ischemic symptoms in the absence of intermediate or high-risk features Cocaine use Chest pain reproduced by palpation From the ACC/AHA guideline update for the management of patients with unstable angina and non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. http://content.onlinejacc.org/article.aspx?articleid=1682681

feature.caption: Clinical pre-test probabilities in patients with stable chest pain symptoms.

figure.caption: Initial diagnostic management of patients with suspected SCAD. CAD ¼ coronary artery disease; CTA ¼ computed tomography angiography; CXR = chest X-ray; ECG = electrocardiogram; ICA = invasive coronary angiography; LVEF = left ventricular ejection fraction; PTP = pre-test probability; SCAD = stable coronary artery disease. aMay be omitted in very young and healthy patients with a high suspicion of an extracardiac cause of chest pain and in multimorbid patients in whom the echo result has no consequence for further patient management. bIf diagnosis of SCAD is doubtful, establishing a diagnosis using pharmacologic stress imaging prior to treatment may be reasonable.

Non-invasive testing in patients with suspected SCAD and an intermediate pre-test probability. CAD = coronary artery disease; CTA = computed tomography angiography; CMR = cardiac magnetic resonance; ECG = electrocardiogram; ICA = invasive coronary angiography; LVEF = left ventricular ejection fraction; PET = positron emission tomography; PTP = pre-test probability; SCAD = stable coronary artery disease; SPECT = single photon emission computed tomography. aConsider age of patient versus radiation exposure. bIn patients unable to exercise, use echo or SPECT/PET with pharmacologic stress instead. cCMR is only performed using pharmacologic stress. dPatient characteristics should make a fully diagnostic coronary CTA scan highly probable. Consider result to be unclear in patients with severe diffuse or focal calcification. eProceed as in lower left coronary CTA box. fProceed as in stress testing for ischaemia box.
